notes.title: Innovation: what it is and its four forms
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- Innovation = something new that **creates value and gets used**.
- Four forms: **product, process, business model, market**.
- Engineers make it possible; this course is about whether it's worth building.

---

## In one line
**Innovation** is the successful introduction of something new (an idea, product, process or business model) that creates value for someone. Being new isn't enough: it has to be used and matter.

## Structure to write
**Four forms of innovation** (slide 4):
1. **Product**: a new or improved offering
2. **Process**: a better way of doing existing work
3. **Business model**: a new way of creating and capturing value
4. **Market**: an existing offering reaching a new audience

**Why engineers need this course** (slide 3):
- See opportunity, not just specs: from "build what's requested" to "spot what's needed"
- Think in prototypes, not perfection: test small, cheap versions first
- Bridge technical and human value: link what you can build to what people will use and pay for

**Engineer's role:** makes innovation technically possible, but technical possibility doesn't guarantee value. The gap is "can build it" vs "should build it".

## Remember it by
**P-P-B-M**: Product, Process, Business model, Market.

*Slides 3–4*

notes.title: Innovation vs invention
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- **Invention** = creating something new. Test: *does it work?*
- **Innovation** = turning an idea into adopted value. Test: *does it get used?*
- Most inventions never become innovations.

---

## In one line
Every innovation may start with an invention, but an invention only becomes an innovation once people actually adopt it.

## Structure to write (comparison table, slide 6)
| Aspect | Invention | Innovation |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | A new device, method or idea | Applying an idea to create adopted value |
| Primary question | "Can this be made?" | "Will this be used, and by whom?" |
| Where it happens | Lab, workshop, research setting | Market, business, real-world deployment |
| Requires | Technical knowledge, creativity | Technical knowledge + market insight + execution |
| Risk of failure | Low (no market exposure yet) | High (must survive customers and competition) |

Extra points (slide 5): invention can sit unused for decades; innovation needs a **business model**, not just a mechanism.

## Examples (slide 7)
| | Invention | Innovation |
|---|---|---|
| Steam engine | 1600s–1700s, pumping water | Railways and factories → Industrial Revolution |
| Telephone | 1876, voice over wire | Decades of network build-out → mobile/smartphones |
| IC engine | 1800s | Ford's moving assembly line made cars affordable |

## Why it matters (slide 8)
Inventing → judge by "does it work reliably?" Innovating → "who needs it, will they adopt it?" Most real projects need both: switch from *make it work* to *make it matter*.

*Slides 5–8*

notes.title: Entrepreneurial mindset: six traits
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- Mindset ≠ starting a company: it's **founder instincts in technical work**.
- Six traits: **curiosity, problem-first, resourcefulness, calibrated risk, user empathy, resilience**.
- Arc: **Notice → Prototype → Validate → Scale**.

---

## In one line
An entrepreneurial mindset means approaching engineering with curiosity about unmet needs, comfort with uncertainty and a bias toward testing ideas in the real world.

## Structure to write
**Traditional vs entrepreneurial engineering** (slide 9)
| Traditional | Entrepreneurial |
|---|---|
| Given a spec, build to it precisely | Questions whether the spec solves a real problem |
| Optimises for correctness and reliability | Optimises for validated value, then reliability |
| Success = technical performance | Success = adoption and impact |

**Six traits** (slide 10)
1. **Technical curiosity**: dig into why a system behaves as it does, not just fix symptoms
2. **Problem-first thinking**: start from a real need, then choose the technology
3. **Resourcefulness**: working prototypes with limited time, budget or tools
4. **Calibrated risk-taking**: small, cheap experiments to test risky assumptions early
5. **User empathy**: how real people will use (or misuse) what you build
6. **Resilience**: failed prototypes and pivots are data, not defeat

**From problem to impact** (slide 11)
1. **Notice**: spot a real, recurring problem
2. **Prototype**: smallest working version that tests the core idea
3. **Validate**: put it in front of real users
4. **Scale**: refine on evidence, grow what's proven

## Remember it by
Traits: **C-P-R-R-U-R** (Curiosity, Problem-first, Resourcefulness, Risk, User empathy, Resilience).

*Slides 9–12*

notes.title: Types of innovation: incremental, disruptive, frugal
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- **Incremental** = improve what exists (low risk).
- **Disruptive** = start with an overlooked segment, then displace the leaders.
- **Frugal** = do more with less by redesigning, not just cutting.

---

## Structure to write
| | Incremental | Disruptive | Frugal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Definition | Small, continuous improvements to an existing product, service or process | New product/service for an overlooked or underserved segment that improves and eventually displaces established competitors | Simpler, more affordable solutions, often for resource-constrained markets, by rethinking design |
| Key traits | Improves efficiency, quality or features; same business model and market; common in mature industries | Starts "worse" by traditional metrics but solves a different problem; creates a new market or value network; leaders dismiss it | Affordability and accessibility; strips to core function without losing essential value; reverse innovation; resourcefulness over big R&D |
| Risk | Lower risk, lower cost, faster | Higher risk, potentially transformative reward | Low cost by design |
| Examples | Yearly iPhone models; flip-top toothpaste cap; better fuel efficiency each model year; app updates (dark mode) | Netflix vs Blockbuster; Uber/Ola vs taxis; digital cameras vs Kodak film; low-cost airlines | Tata Nano; Jaipur Foot; M-Pesa (Kenya); Aakash tablet |

**Reverse innovation:** a frugal innovation from an emerging market later moves into developed markets (slide 7).

## Classifying (slide 9)
Justify the type in one sentence; many real innovations **blend types**. From the deck's sorting list: new bristle pattern → incremental; SaaS replacing boxed software → disruptive; solar lanterns for off-grid villages → frugal; budget phone stripped of extras → frugal; new snack flavour → incremental; rural telemedicine app → frugal and disruptive.

## Takeaway (slide 12)
No one-size-fits-all: the right type depends on **goal, resources and market**, and big breakthroughs often combine all three.

*Types of Innovation deck, slides 1–12*

notes.title: Design thinking: definition and the three Ps
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- Human-centred approach: **needs first, problems as opportunities, test before committing**.
- Aim for **desirable + feasible + viable**.
- People → desirability, Process → feasibility, Purpose → viability.

---

## In one line
**Design thinking** is a human-centred approach to innovation that puts real people's needs first, reframes problems as opportunities and rapidly tests ideas before committing to them.

## Structure to write (slide 3)
| P | Lens | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **People** | Desirability | Understand users deeply through empathy and observation |
| **Process** | Feasibility | Iterate quickly: build, test, learn, refine |
| **Purpose** | Viability | Deliver value that is sustainable for the business |

The sweet spot every solution aims for: **desirable, feasible and viable**.

*EM Unit 2 deck, slides 1–3*

notes.title: Five stages of design thinking; diverge vs converge
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- **Empathize → Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test**.
- It's a **loop**: Test feeds back into Define and Ideate.
- Diverge = go wide (Empathize, Ideate, Prototype); converge = go narrow (Define, Select, Test).

---

## Structure to write (slide 4)
1. **Empathize**: understand users' needs, emotions and context
2. **Define**: synthesise insights into a clear problem statement
3. **Ideate**: generate a wide range of possible solutions
4. **Prototype**: quick, low-cost representations of ideas
5. **Test**: try prototypes with users and gather feedback

**Non-linear:** insights from Test go back into Define and Ideate, so it's a cycle, not a straight line.

## Diverge, then converge (slide 5)
| Diverge: expand possibilities | Converge: make focused choices |
|---|---|
| Empathize: gather many perspectives | Define: one sharp problem statement |
| Ideate: lots of ideas | Select: cluster and prioritise ideas |
| Prototype: explore multiple concepts | Test: validate and decide what stays |
| Defer judgment, seek quantity and variety | Analyse, prioritise, commit |

## Remember it by
**"Every Developer Is Probably Tired"**: Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test.

*EM Unit 2 deck, slides 4–5*

notes.title: Problem identification and framing techniques
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- Solve the **right** problem before solving it right.
- Rules: **root cause, user's problem, evidence, narrow**.
- Tools: **5 Whys, How Might We, Point-of-View, problem statement**.

---

## In one line
Most failed products are well-built answers to the wrong question, so frame the problem before solving it.

## Structure to write
**Four rules** (slide 6)
1. **Symptom vs root cause**: look past what's visible to what's causing it
2. **User's problem, not yours**: frame it from the user's perspective
3. **Evidence over assumption**: ground it in observation and data
4. **Narrow and specific**: a focused problem is a solvable one

**Why it matters:** ~35% of startups fail because there was no real market need; fixing a problem framed correctly up front is ~5× cheaper than after build; one sharp statement aligns the team.

**Four framing techniques** (slide 7)
| Technique | What it does | Deck example |
|---|---|---|
| **5 Whys** | Ask "why?" repeatedly to drill from symptom to root cause | Why is checkout slow? → … → the API retries 3× on timeout |
| **How Might We** | Turn a pain point into an open, optimistic question | "How might we make first-time setup feel effortless?" |
| **Point-of-View** | User + need + insight in one sentence | "A busy nurse needs fast handoffs because errors cost lives." |
| **Problem statement** | Concise, testable definition and scope | "Users abandon onboarding at step 3 due to unclear input rules." |

*EM Unit 2 deck, slides 6–7*

notes.title: Problem–solution fit and validating it
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- Fit = a **validated problem** meets a solution that **really resolves it** for a defined group.
- Comes **before product–market fit**.
- Validate: **segment → pain → map → signal → measure**.

---

## In one line
**Problem–solution fit** is the point where a validated problem meets a solution that genuinely resolves it for a defined group of users. It comes before product–market fit.

## Structure to write
**Three conditions** (slide 8)
1. **Real, urgent problem**: people already look for workarounds
2. **Clear target segment**: you know exactly whose problem it is
3. **Solution resolves it**: measurably better than the alternatives

**Five steps to validate** (slide 9)
1. **Define the segment**: the customers who feel the pain most
2. **Confirm the pain**: interview users; look for workarounds and willingness to pay
3. **Map the solution**: sketch how it removes the pain, end to end
4. **Test with a signal**: landing page, prototype or concierge MVP to measure real interest
5. **Measure and decide**: adoption, retention, satisfaction → pivot or persevere

**Signal to look for:** users are disappointed when they can't use your solution.

*EM Unit 2 deck, slides 8–9*

notes.title: Ideation: brainstorming, SCAMPER, mind mapping
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- **Brainstorming**: quantity, build on others, defer criticism.
- **SCAMPER**: Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to other use, Eliminate, Reverse.
- **Mind map**: central theme → branches → sub-branches.

---

## Brainstorming (slide 11)
**Seven ground rules:** defer judgment; encourage wild ideas; go for quantity; build on ideas ("yes, and…"); stay focused on the How-Might-We; one conversation at a time; be visual.

**Running a session:** 1 **Frame** (open with a clear HMW) → 2 **Diverge** (silent solo ideas, then share) → 3 **Cluster** (group into themes) → 4 **Vote** (dot-vote) → 5 **Refine** (develop top picks into concepts).

## SCAMPER (slide 12)
| Letter | Prompt | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| S | Substitute | Swap a component, material or person |
| C | Combine | Merge two ideas, steps or features |
| A | Adapt | Adjust an idea from another context |
| M | Modify | Magnify, minify or reshape an element |
| P | Put to other use | Apply it to a new purpose or market |
| E | Eliminate | Remove parts to simplify |
| R | Reverse | Flip the order, roles or direction |

## Mind mapping (slide 13)
Start with the **central theme** in the middle → **branch** main ideas outward → add **sub-branches** for detail → **one keyword** per branch → **colour and images** to aid recall → **link** related branches.

## The whole flow (slide 14)
Identify the problem → Empathize & Define → Ideate (brainstorm, SCAMPER, mind map) → validate fit, and loop back when testing sharpens the problem.

*EM Unit 2 deck, slides 10–15*

notes.title: EM Unit 1 — one-page revision sheet
notes.content:
**No exam pattern announced yet.** Write answers as *definition → structure (list or table) → one example*.

| Topic | The structure to reproduce | Slides |
|---|---|---|
| Innovation | new + creates value + gets used; Product, Process, Business model, Market | EM 3–4 |
| Invention vs innovation | table: nature, question, where, requires, risk; steam engine / telephone / IC engine | EM 5–8 |
| Mindset | traditional vs entrepreneurial table; six traits; Notice → Prototype → Validate → Scale | EM 9–11 |
| Types | incremental / disruptive / frugal: definition, traits, 2 examples each; reverse innovation | Innovation 3–12 |

**One-liners**
- Invention asks "can this be made?"; innovation asks "will this be used, and by whom?"
- Six traits: curiosity, problem-first, resourcefulness, calibrated risk, user empathy, resilience.
- Incremental = improve what exists · disruptive = change the game · frugal = do more with less.

notes.content:

| Five stages | Empathize → Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test, a loop; diverge vs converge table | 4–5 |
| Problem identification | 4 rules (root cause, user's problem, evidence, narrow); 5 Whys, HMW, POV, problem statement | 6–7 |

| Ideation | brainstorming 7 rules + Frame/Diverge/Cluster/Vote/Refine; SCAMPER; mind map | 10–13 |

**One-liners**
- Solving the right problem matters more than solving a problem right.
- POV = user + need + insight.
- Fit signal: users are disappointed when they can't use your solution.
